days.reason: The day is directly named after and defined by the parable of the sower (Matt 13:1-23). The text contains the parable itself and Jesus' explanation of how God's word is received in different hearts.

The parable of the weeds in the field is a central part of the chapter, often preached together with the parable of the sower on this day to illustrate the growth of God's kingdom and the final judgment.
The parables of the mustard seed and the yeast are part of the same teaching session in Matt 13 that is preached on Sower Sunday, illustrating the growth of the kingdom of heaven.
The transitional verses summarizing Jesus' use of parables and linking it to prophecy (Isa 6:9-10) are an integral part of the chapter's theological message on Sower Sunday.
Jesus' explanation of the parable of the weeds (continued from verse 24), which expands on the theme of judgment and the nature of God's kingdom, is a natural part of the reading for Sower Sunday.

The parables of the treasure in the field, the pearl of great value, and the net are part of the same chapter (Matt 13) and deal with the value of the kingdom of heaven and the final separation, often read together on this day.
The conclusion of the chapter with Jesus' rejection in his hometown shows the consequence of not understanding the parables and is a natural ending to the reading for the day.
The parable of the weeds deals centrally with the final judgment and the separation at the end of the world, a main theme for Judgment Sunday.
Jesus' explanation of the weeds describes the mechanism of judgment (angels, furnace of fire, separation), which is central to Judgment Sunday.
The parable of the net describes the final judgment and the separation between the good and the bad, a central theme for Judgment Sunday.

_versions.reason: [critical] Verses 34-35 are omitted in the tagging. These verses serve as an important transition and theological summary of the entire parable chapter (the purpose of the parables and fulfillment of prophecy). They should be included in the primary or secondary part of Sower Sunday to provide a complete picture of the chapter's structure.; [minor] Verses 53-58 (Jesus' rejection in his hometown) are omitted. Although this is a new scene, it is a direct consequence of the parables and Jesus' teaching in chapter 13. It is common to read this as an ending to the chapter on Sower Sunday to show the reaction to his teaching. It should be added as a secondary part.; [minor] The parables of the weeds (24-30, 36-43) and the net (47-50) deal centrally with the final judgment and the separation between the righteous and the wicked. These have a strong connection to Judgment Sunday (Christ the King), even though they are primarily preached on Sower Sunday. It may be useful to mark these parts with 'secondary' relevance for Judgment Sunday to cover the chapter's themes of judgment.
